sample.name: Pigeonhole Principle
sample.definition: A counting principle stating that if more objects are assigned to fewer containers, at least one container must contain more than one object.
sample.scope: Applies to finite counting and allocation arguments in which the number of objects exceeds the number of available categories or containers; it does not by itself identify which container contains the repeated objects.
sample.semantic_description: A foundational counting principle that converts a simple cardinality inequality into a guaranteed existence result. It is used in combinatorics, discrete mathematics, hashing arguments, and allocation reasoning.
sample.keywords_synonyms: Pigeonhole principle; Dirichlet principle; box principle

sample.name: Functional Diversity and Adaptive Capacity
sample.definition: Functional diversity and adaptive capacity describe the sustainability value of maintaining sufficiently varied components, roles, capabilities or response strategies so that a system can continue functioning, adapt, or recover when conditions change. Diversity matters here because different components may respond differently to the same disturbance, provide complementary functions, or provide alternatives when one pathway fails.
sample.scope: Applies when variation among components has a demonstrable or plausible functional relationship to resilience, adaptation, recovery, or response diversity. The relevant unit of diversity may be biological species, functional traits, technologies, infrastructure pathways, organizations, knowledge sources, or other system components. Diversity is not inherently sustainable: additional components can also increase resource demand, coordination burden, incompatibility, or risk.
sample.core_ideas: Maintain useful variation; preserve functional redundancy where failure is consequential; combine complementary capabilities; avoid unnecessary monocultures or single-path dependencies; assess the cost of diversity against its resilience benefit; distinguish diversity itself from the functions diversity enables.
sample.semantic_description: The principle connects biodiversity and other forms of system diversity to the ability to absorb disturbance, adapt and recover.
sample.keywords_synonyms: biodiversity; diversity; redundancy; resilience; adaptive capacity
sample.sustainability_principle: A system should preserve diversity where diversity provides the variation, redundancy or complementary functions needed to remain resilient under changing conditions.
sample.underlying_mechanism: Diverse components can respond differently to disturbance, reducing the chance that one failure disables the whole system.
sample.derived_from_practice_or_system: Biodiversity and resilient ecological systems; diverse agricultural and social systems.
sample.evidence_status: UN SDG 15; IPCC AR6 sustainability and resilience literature.
sample.transferability: Agriculture; ecology; infrastructure; organizations; data/AI; communities
sample.boundary_conditions: Diversity should not be treated as inherently beneficial if it creates unmanaged hazards or unnecessary complexity.
sample.recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when the graph contains diversity, redundancy, modularity, biodiversity or resilience concepts; strengthen only when the application context shows functional diversity matters.
sample.:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

sample.name: Textile Repair and Reuse Before Recycling
sample.description: Textile Repair and Reuse Before Recycling applies where Premature disposal or recycling of textile products that can still provide useful service. The operational response is Repair and reuse of textile products before recycling. The mechanism is Repair and reuse are used to retain product/material value before disposal or recycling. The intended sustainability outcome is Reduced resource demand and waste through extended use.
sample.technical_problem: Premature disposal or recycling of textile products that can still provide useful service.
sample.operational_action: Repair and reuse of textile products before recycling
sample.mechanism: Repair and reuse are used to retain product/material value before disposal or recycling
sample.sustainability_outcome: Reduced resource demand and waste through extended use
sample.boundary_conditions: Use only where repair or reuse can safely retain meaningful function; do not prefer extended use when safety, health, or performance is compromised.
sample.relevant_disciplines: Textile Engineering; Product Design; Materials Engineering; Industrial Design
sample.transferability: Cross-disciplinary where technical applicability and boundary conditions are satisfied
sample.keywords_synonyms: textile repair and reuse before recycling; repair and reuse are used to retain product/material value before disposal or recycling
